record.paper_title: Stellar model calibrations with the Ai Phe binary system. Open questions about the robustness of the fit
record.original_question: For the detached eclipsing binary system Ai Phe, whose primary star has already undergone first dredge-up while the secondary has not, how robust are stellar-model calibrations—especially the inferred system age and the convective core overshooting parameter β—to assumptions about microscopic diffusion and surface metallicity evolution? More specifically, if microscopic diffusion is allowed to alter the observable surface [Fe/H] of the stars versus being effectively canceled at the surface by competing mixing processes, do the same precise masses, radii, temperatures, and metallicity measurements lead to materially different calibrations?

evidence.quote: Aims. Relying on recently available and very precise observational data for the Ai Phe binary system, we explore the robustness of the calibration of stellar models achievable with this system.

a firm prediction of the surface metallicity for stars in the mass range of Ai Phe before the first dredge-up is problematic. This poses an interesting question as to the robustness of the fit obtained for similar systems

The comparison of the calibrations obtained under the two scenarios allows us to investigate their robustness to different choices of the efficiency of the microscopic diffusion in this critical mass range.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a detached double-lined eclipsing binary system in which both components have precisely measured masses $M_1, M_2$, radii $R_1, R_2$, effective temperatures $T_{\mathrm{eff},1}, T_{\mathrm{eff},2}$, and a measured surface metallicity $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]_{\mathrm{surf}}$. Assume the more massive primary has already completed the first dredge-up (so its convective envelope has homogenized inner material with the surface), while the less massive secondary has not yet undergone first dredge-up. Stellar evolution models depend on, among other parameters, a common age $t$ for the two stars and a convective core overshooting parameter $\beta$ (which sets the extension $\ell_{\mathrm{ov}} = \beta H_p$ of mixing beyond the Schwarzschild boundary, where $H_p$ is the local pressure scale height). A calibration consists of finding $(t,\beta,\text{initial composition},\dots)$ for which a pair of stellar tracks simultaneously reproduces the measured $(M_i,R_i,T_{\mathrm{eff},i},[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]_{\mathrm{surf}})$.

Two physical scenarios are considered for the treatment of microscopic diffusion (gravitational settling and radiative levitation of metals) in the radiative envelopes of stars in the relevant mass range:
(A) microscopic diffusion is fully active and is allowed to modify the present-day surface $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]$ relative to the initial composition;
(B) microscopic diffusion is included in the interior, but its effect on the surface abundance is canceled by a competing mixing process (e.g., turbulent mixing or radiative levitation) so that the surface $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]$ effectively tracks the initial composition prior to first dredge-up.

Question: Given the same set of precise observational constraints $(M_i,R_i,T_{\mathrm{eff},i},[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]_{\mathrm{surf}})$, do calibrations performed under scenarios (A) and (B) yield statistically consistent inferred values of the system age $t$ and the overshooting parameter $\beta$, or do they produce materially different best-fit values and confidence regions? Quantify the robustness of the inferred $(t,\beta)$ to the assumed efficiency of microscopic diffusion at the surface in this mass regime.
artifact.status_search_result: The question concerns a methodological/astrophysical robustness issue about stellar model calibrations for stars near the first-dredge-up mass range. No definitive resolution has been established: the surface effect of microscopic diffusion versus competing mixing in this mass range is recognized as an outstanding modeling uncertainty, and recent literature continues to report calibration ambiguities for systems such as AI Phe rather than a settled answer.
